surfaces.title: Sleepless Night
surfaces.creator: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (French, 1864–1901)
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Sleepless Night is indexed from Cleveland Museum Open Access API. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec experimented with the recently invented technique of lithography. In addition to fine art prints, he often created ephemera, including posters and sheet music—such as this example. It was commissioned as a cover illustration for Nuit Blanche , a poem by Jean Goudezki that was set to music composed by Désiré Dihau, a well-known bassoonist.

surfaces.title: Sculptress
surfaces.creator: Eugène Grasset (French, 1841–1917)
surfaces.medium: lithograph with watercolor added by hand
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Sculptress is indexed from Cleveland Museum Open Access API. Grasset, greatly influenced by the art of Japan, Persia, and Egypt, created designs for stained glass windows, furniture, tapestries, and fabrics. This female allegory of Sculpture was meant for an 1898 exhibition poster. Only the black areas and lines were printed. Rather than using a separate stone to print each color, watercolor was applied with the aid of a stencil.

surfaces.descriptionSummary: Two Covered Boxes, One with Tassels is indexed from Cooper Hewitt. Two square-shaped boxes, designed as product packaging, are framed in actual or simulated wooden or metallic material. Eight foliate forms in brown on a black background are arranged around the four sides of the box covers. One cover design features an additional foliate in the center and five knotted black tassels attached to the rim; the other has a centered circle of the same material as the rim. The boxes are displayed on a striped chevron-patterned fabric background.

surfaces.descriptionSummary: Alfa Laval separator reklam.jpg is an openly licensed Commons image record. Company advertising poster from early 1900 when the company name was AB Separator, founded by Gustaf de Laval , manufacturing separators for separating cream from milk. The painting shows how easy it is with small efforts to separate the cream from the milk by a manually driven separator from the company Separator AB, later Alfa-Laval. The milk and cream coming out from two different tubes. The fresh cream was particular appreciated by the cat.

This optimistic poster promises disabled veterans that they can still live a happy and productive life through labor. Vignettes of amputees employing new prosthetic limbs in various factory and agricultural trades…

surfaces.title: A cobbler who doesn't wear shoes. This hole in the wall is a typical cobbler's shop at Skoplje, Serbia. His own shoeless feet wouldn't be considered a very good advertisement for his trade in America. But he has all the trade that he can take care of as leather is mighty scarce. He didn't mind because the American Red Cross brought several thousand pairs of shoes into the Balkans for distribution to the needy. He says, he realizes the soles will wear out sometime and that means more trade for him

surfaces.descriptionSummary: Four Male Heads in Ancient Roman Style is indexed from Cooper Hewitt. Four heads, three in frontal view and one in profile, are lightly sketched in the right half, and are labeled in ancient Roman-style capital letters. The heads are styled in the manner of ancient Roman sculpture or coin portraiture. On the top left, the head of a young man, turned toward the left, is dressed in wavy hair cascading down the right, and shows vestiges of a laurel wreath on top. He is identified as Caligula, imprinted next to the head on the top right. On the right, slightly below, the head of a mature man is abbreviated by the right edge of the page. A fund-raising poster for the Zonnestraal ("Sunbeam") sanatorium for the tuberculous in Hilversum, founded in 1928 by the diamond merchant Jan van Zutphen, originally for tuberculous people working in the diamond industry. A fund-raising poster for the Zonnestraal ("Sunbeam") sanatorium for the tuberculous in Hilversum, founded in 1928 by the diamond merchant Jan van Zutphen, originally for tuberculous people working in the diamond industry. surfaces.descriptionSummary: By the Rushy - Fringed Bank is indexed from Art Institute of Chicago API. Edward McKnight Kauffer often changed his style to suit a poster’s subject. This work does not say anything about how and when to use the Underground. Rather, the company had it created simply to please those entering or passing by a station where it was displayed. One of four posters illustrating lines from English poets, it uses washes of color to create a landscape evocative of John Milton’s verse.

surfaces.descriptionSummary: Tuberculosis patients lying on their beds in a crowded tuberculosis hospital; advertising a tombola in aid of tuberculosis sufferers in L'Hérault, France. Top, a roundel showing tuberculosis patients lying on their beds in a crowded TB hospital, with the windows wide open at night. Top right, the sun coming out through the clouds. Below, the text describes the distress of tuberculosis, which brings an end to the joys of life. Cure is possible, but it is tedious and…
surfaces.sourceDescription: Top, a roundel showing tuberculosis patients lying on their beds in a crowded TB hospital, with the windows wide open at night. Top right, the sun coming out through the clouds. Below, the text describes the distress of tuberculosis, which brings an end to the joys of life. Cure is possible, but it is tedious and demoralising. An appeal is made to the public to support the lottery organized by, and for, the tuberculous patients of the Bellevue and Bon Accueil sanatoriums of L'Hérault. The prizes include 1933 models of a Peugeot car and a Peugeot motorcycle

surfaces.sourceDescription: The Papers, 1933-1981, of Stetson Kennedy comprise correspondence; subject files on various organizations, individuals, and ideas; typescripts of articles written by Kennedy; newsclippings; press releases; bulletins and fliers; pamphlets; periodicals; and photographs. The subject files pertain to economic conditions, labor and anti-black violence, peace groups, peonage, Southern politicians, Mexico, the Spanish Civil War, and Kennedy's own campaign for a U.S. Senate seat from Florida in 1950. Articles, clippings, and pamphlets concern civil rights, international affairs, the Ku Klux Klan, labor (particularly CIO) organizing, and southern politics. The photographs depict WPA work in progress, attacks against Negroes (including lynching), and various organizations. The many periodicals include two issues (1947) of Eugene Talmadge's The Statesman, twenty-one issues (1943-1950) of The Southern Patriot, and eight issues (1939-1943) of Lillian Smith's North Georgia Review. surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary:
'You are helping by carrying your shopping' poster is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. This poster was printed in Britain during the Second World War (1939-45) to remind people to conserve fuel resources which were rationed. 
 
 It was donated to Te Papa by Wellington businessman Mr Cecil H. Andrews. He collected many such posters during the war and distributed them to his clients for display in their shop windows, such as McKenzies, James Smith’s and Woolworths. surfaces.sourceDescription:
This poster was printed in Britain during the Second World War (1939-45) to remind people to conserve fuel resources which were rationed. 
 
 It was donated to Te Papa by Wellington businessman Mr Cecil H. Andrews. He collected many such posters during the war and distributed them to his clients for display in their shop windows, such as McKenzies, James Smith’s and Woolworths. This particular poster would have been just as resonant in New Zealand as in Britain, as petrol was rationed here from 1939-46. 
 
 The poster shows an ordinary person going about their business, which is often a feature of Second World War posters. Civilians were frequently targeted by government campaigns – to volunteer for service, to give money, to recycle and conserve resources. In the Second World War everyone was expected to play a part, and it would have been hard to escape the direct appeal of colourful posters like this on city streets.

 It was donated to Te Papa by Wellington businessman Mr Cecil H. Andrews. He collected many such posters during the war and distributed them to his clients for display in their shop windows, such as McKenzies, James Smith’s and Woolworths. This particular poster would have been just as resonant in New Zealand as in Britain, as petrol was rationed here from 1939-46. 
 
 The poster shows an ordinary person going about their business, which is often a feature of Second World War posters. Civilians were frequently targeted by government campaigns – to volunteer for service, to give money, to recycle and conserve resources. In the Second World War everyone was expected to play a part, and it would have been hard to escape the direct appeal of colourful posters like this on city streets.

surfaces.sourceDescription: \n This poster was one of the first voluntary recruitment posters to be commissioned by the Army Department at the beginning of the Second World War. It was critical for the government to stimulate enthusiasm for voluntary enlistment, partly in the hope of avoiding conscription. The strongly gendered image and message in this poster appealed to masculine ideals of work, honour and commitment. Here war equals work, and a regular soldier does the calling, not the government. \n Very few examples of this poster have survived, and very few are held in public institutions. With the introduction of compulsory military service in June 1940, recruitment posters 'were of course abandoned, and except for a few copies retained for historical purposes no special effort was made to preserve them' (Director of Publicity to C. H. Bateson, 24 April 1941, External Affairs, series 1, 84/12/12, part 1, Archives New Zealand).

\n This poster was one of the first voluntary recruitment posters to be commissioned by the Army Department at the beginning of the Second World War. It was critical for the government to stimulate enthusiasm for voluntary enlistment, partly in the hope of avoiding conscription. The strongly gendered image and message in this poster appealed to masculine ideals of work, honour and commitment. Here war equals work, and a regular soldier does the calling, not the government. \n Very few examples of this poster have survived, and very few are held in public institutions. With the introduction of compulsory military service in June 1940, recruitment posters 'were of course abandoned, and except for a few copies retained for historical purposes no special effort was made to preserve them' (Director of Publicity to C. H. Bateson, 24 April 1941, External Affairs, series 1, 84/12/12, part 1, Archives New Zealand).

surfaces.descriptionSummary: Poster, 'Great Britain will pursue' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. On 7 December 1941, Japan launched a series of attacks on British and American territories in Asia and the Pacific. The attacks shocked the world, although fears about Japan's imperialist aims had in fact been growing for decades. \n The Fall of Singapore sent shockwaves around the British Empire. More than 130,000 troops laid down their arms when the Allies surrendered in Singapore on 15 February, 1942, and Winston Churchill later described it as 'the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history'. Two years later, his words declare British resolve to 'pursue the War Against Japan to the very end'.

surfaces.sourceDescription: The Papers, 1933-1981, of Stetson Kennedy comprise correspondence; subject files on various organizations, individuals, and ideas; typescripts of articles written by Kennedy; newsclippings; press releases; bulletins and fliers; pamphlets; periodicals; and photographs. The subject files pertain to economic conditions, labor and anti-black violence, peace groups, peonage, Southern politicians, Mexico, the Spanish Civil War, and Kennedy's own campaign for a U.S. Senate seat from Florida in 1950. Articles, clippings, and pamphlets concern civil rights, international affairs, the Ku Klux Klan, labor (particularly CIO) organizing, and southern politics. The photographs depict WPA work in progress, attacks against Negroes (including lynching), and various organizations. The many periodicals include two issues (1947) of Eugene Talmadge's The Statesman, twenty-one issues (1943-1950) of The Southern Patriot, and eight issues (1939-1943) of Lillian Smith's North Georgia Review. surfaces.sourceDescription: The New Zealand government financed the Second World War (1930-45) from internal resources, raising substantial amounts through taxation, internal loans and savings. Posters such as this one played a significant part in the associated fund-raising campaigns, making intense appeals to New Zealanders' sense of patriotism and sacrifice. This particular poster was part of a National Savings movement begun by the New Zealand Government in October 1940 to develop a 'thrift' habit among citizens. The Minister of Finance entrusted the administration of the National Savings Act 1940 to a special committee - the New Zealand National Savings Committee. The National Savings Committee delegated the development of the campaign to the Post Office, but the general scheme and the national publicity arrangements remained with the Committee (including the publishing of posters such as this example).

The New Zealand government financed the Second World War (1930-45) from internal resources, raising substantial amounts through taxation, internal loans and savings. Posters such as this one played a significant part in the associated fund-raising campaigns, making intense appeals to New Zealanders' sense of patriotism and sacrifice. This particular poster was part of a National Savings movement begun by the New Zealand Government in October 1940 to develop a 'thrift' habit among citizens. The Minister of Finance entrusted the administration of the National Savings Act 1940 to a special committee - the New Zealand National Savings Committee. The National Savings Committee delegated the development of the campaign to the Post Office, but the general scheme and the national publicity arrangements remained with the Committee (including the publishing of posters such as this example).

surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Poster, 'Come on - New Zealand!' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. This poster was one of 150,000 posters, window stickers, grille cards and strips produced in 31 different designs and sizes for the New Zealand government's Victory Loan campaign of 1944. The Victory Loan aimed to raise £40 million over a five-week period (28 August to 4 October) to help meet the costs of New Zealand's war expenditure (which was at its highest in the year of 1943-44). \n The posters, including this one, were described as 'Campaign Ammunition' and were widely seen in shop and business windows, railway stations, hotel lobbies, post offices, sport gatherings and campaign meetings.

surfaces.sourceDescription:
This Second World War poster was one of 150,000 posters, window stickers, grille cards and strips produced in 31 different designs and sizes for the Victory Loan campaign of August 1944. The Victory Loan aimed to raise £40 million over a five-week period (28 August to 4 October) to help meet the costs of New Zealand's war expenditure, which was at its highest in the year of 1943-44. 
 This poster was considered 'campaign ammunition' and would have been seen in shop and business windows, railway stations, hotel lobbies, post offices, sport gatherings and campaign meetings. The large scale of the Victory Loan required a 'Campaign Handbook' which detailed the importance of posters and how to use them. 
 The image in this poster is particularly romantic with its heroic-looking airman gazing up at the machinery of war in the sky.

rows: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

This Second World War poster was one of 150,000 posters, window stickers, grille cards and strips produced in 31 different designs and sizes for the Victory Loan campaign of August 1944. The Victory Loan aimed to raise £40 million over a five-week period (28 August to 4 October) to help meet the costs of New Zealand's war expenditure, which was at its highest in the year of 1943-44. 
 This poster was considered 'campaign ammunition' and would have been seen in shop and business windows, railway stations, hotel lobbies, post offices, sport gatherings and campaign meetings. The large scale of the Victory Loan required a 'Campaign Handbook' which detailed the importance of posters and how to use them. 
 The image in this poster is particularly romantic with its heroic-looking airman gazing up at the machinery of war in the sky.

Elizabeth Catlett and Alberto Beltrán were two of the most adept artists to join the Taller de Gráfica Popular in the post–World War II period, and this large, two-sheet print embodies the collaborative work that continued to be so central to the workshop’s practice, as well as the antiwar causes to which the Taller was particularly devoted during the 1950s. surfaces.descriptionSummary: Anti-CIO political poster from Eastman, Georgia, circa 1946. is indexed from GSU Library Digital Collections. Text on poster: "Shall These Men Tell You What To Do? George Baldanzi of New York, on the right, is vice-president of the TWUA (CIO) and is vice-chairman of the drive in Southern Textile mills. On the left is a man called SMITH (probably Smithkowlski) of San Francisco, California, who is the big shot chairman of the drive in the State of North Carolina. Look at them... take a good look, employees of the Eastman mill... do you think they want to help you, and YOU? Can't You Just See Yourself Crushed Under the Thumbs of These Fellows if You Vote C.I.O.? Let's Vote…
surfaces.sourceDescription: Text on poster: "Shall These Men Tell You What To Do? Look at them... take a good look, employees of the Eastman mill... do you think they want to help you, and YOU? Can't You Just See Yourself Crushed Under the Thumbs of These Fellows if You Vote C.I.O.? Let's Vote 'Em Out of Eastman, Ga." surfaces.sourceDescription: Shot in Cape Town, South Africa, this film was originally silent with a voice-over sound track added later. The film shows the surgical resection of three ribs and apicolysis followed by resection of four ribs and apicolysis. surfaces.sourceDescription: A traffic safety poster from the late 1950s. Top row, three small pictures showing the correct way to observe traffic regulations. This is followed by three cartoon-style stories (each with 4 or 5 pictures) of tales illustrating the dangers and unfortunate results of not observing the rules: first, a man, his wife and their two children all try to travel on one bicycle, but the father, who is driving, is distracted by a pedestrian and by rain, leading to a collision in which they are all badly wounded; second, two men driving a horse and cart negligently allow the horse to be frightened by a car, leading to overturning of the cart; third, a man falls asleep on his horse-drawn cart which is…

surfaces.sourceDescription: Georgia State Signal, volume 18, number 9 [misnumbered 8] (February 2, 1960). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

surfaces.sourceDescription: The Georgia State College Signal, volume 24, number 25 (April 28, 1966). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

surfaces.sourceDescription: The Georgia State College Signal, volume 27, number 6 (October 10, 1968). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

The Great Speckled Bird was published from 1968 to 1976 with some issues appearing in the 1980s and 2000s. surfaces.sourceDescription: Caption: "Walter Botts during 1971 Atlanta visit. Famous poster poser dies in California. August 11, 1972." Caption: "Striking his Uncle Sam Pose. In 1938, artist James Montgomery Flagg was drawing an Army recruiting poster, and he asked Walter Botts, a musician, to pose as Uncle Sam. 'What do you want to do with your hands?' asked Flagg. 'Why don't I point my finger like this and say, 'I Want You?' Botts suggested, cupping his lips as he pronounced 'you.' 'No. Frown,' said Flagg. The result was the familiar poster that invited young men into the Army during World War II and for years afterwards. Visiting Atlanta for the grand opening of Uncle Sam's Newsroom Restaurant and Lounge, Botts, now 71, struck that famous pose again Thursday. Staff Photo Bill Grimes. August 6, 1971 Constitution."

Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization records

The Central Office Files (1967-1984) contain correspondence and other materials generated and received by the PATCO central office in Washington, DC. Topics include overtime, strike contingency plans, regional re-alignment, air safety, substance abuse, and medical issues. This series also includes vice-presidential (1977-1981) and presidential (1977-1981) correspondence and executive board resolutions (1969-1981). See Series VI: Central Office Files finding aid for complete description.

surfaces.sourceName: Georgia State University Library Digital Collections / CONTENTdm
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Great Speckled Bird v. 5 no. 26 (July 3, 1972) is indexed from GSU Library Digital Collections. The Great Speckled Bird was published from 1968 to 1976 with some issues appearing in the 1980s and 2000s. This publication was one of the longest-running and highest quality underground newspapers of the era. Frequently published were articles on Atlanta's political leaders, the women's movement, abortion, racial issues, popular culture and gay liberation.

This NADOC [now NAIDOC] poster reflects the decision of the Committee to transition from a day of demonstration to a week- long celebration of the history, culture and achievements of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. The posters title 'Cultural Revival is Survival' represents the decision to introduce ideas of culture and history into what had become predominantly politically based themes for the posters.

surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary:
'Poor & Ignored' poster is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. 
 This poster was produced by a community group involved with the Wellington Unemployed Workers Union, and was printed with the help of the Wellington Media Collective. 
 Wellington Media Collective collaborated with the community to produce the poster as they were not trained artists. This was in line with WMC's philosophy: 'we will work with you, but not for you' (1979). 
 Working with the Collective meant that groups with very few resources could still produce powerful imagery and messaging, particularly those who were more likely to experience unemployment because of discrimination.

surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Poster, 'Hiroshima Day March' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. This poster advertises a march for a Hiroshima Day in the 1980s. At the end of the Second World War, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Both cities were devastated. At least 70,000 people were killed instantly in the Hiroshima blast and 40,000 instantly in the Nagasaki blast, with tens of thousands more dying or suffering from radiation in years to come. These atomic bombs were the first to be used in war and they kick-started the nuclear-arms race.

surfaces.title: Poster, 'Stop French N Tests'
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary:
Poster, 'Stop French N Tests' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. This poster was made by Greenpeace in protest against French nuclear testing in the Pacific. 
 Between 1966 and 1996, France carried out about 190 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia. These caused reef damage, landslides, subsidence, radioactive emissions, and fish poisoning. 
 Greenpeace 
 Greenpeace was founded in 1971 in response to nuclear weapons testing by the United States. In 1972, Greenpeace held its first protest against French testing at Moruroa.

Blair was part of Auckland Artists Action which began as Artists Against Apartheid during the Springbok rugby tour in 1981. The 'AAA' logo bottom right of the poster, was designed by Stanley Pal

surfaces.sourceDescription:
This poster presents an ironic map of the world according to United States President Ronald Reagan (1981-89). Nothing is geographically correct, but possibly how many believed it to be in the 1980s. The world is divided between Republicans ('and other real Americans'); those who are useful politically or economically (eg 'Our Oil'); and everyone else (eg 'Democrats and Welfare Bums'). 
 Many nations do not count in this world view. New Zealand is simply attached to Australia with both being dismissed as 'Kangaroos'. 
 During Ronald Reagan's first term, the Cold War was the most pressing foreign policy issue. He embarked on a massive build-up of weapons and troops. In 1983, he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan aiming to develop space-based weapons to protect America from attacks by Soviet nuclear missiles.

surfaces.sourceDescription: The Georgia State University Signal, volume 39, number 33 (April 28, 1981). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

surfaces.title: 'International Women's Day for Nuclear Disarmament' poster
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary:
'International Women's Day for Nuclear Disarmament' poster is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. 
 This poster was produced for a demonstration in Wellington on 24 May 1983 when a large group of women roped themselves around the perimeter of the Department of Defence headquarters building in Stout Street, Wellington. Their protest was peaceful and was part of the International Women’s Day for Nuclear Disarmament (which had originated in Europe). 
 Impact of protest 
 According to a Defence staff member who was in the building at the time, this was an emotional moment. The men in the office were 'full of bravado' but when the women linked hands, they fell silent.

surfaces.sourceDescription: \n This poster protested against the visit of the USS Texas to Wellington on 10 August 1983. Over 10,000 people marched in a lunch-time protest during the ship's visit, including School Children Against the Texas (SCAT). Posters and slogans were plastered up throughout the city. \n The poster was created by the Coalition Against Nuclear Warships (CANWAR, founded in 1976) which was a coalition of peace groups opposed to nuclear-armed or powered ships visiting New Zealand ports. For example, Wellington received five such visits between 1976 and 1984: USS Truxton in August 1976, September 1980 and May 1982; the USS Texas in August 1983; and the HMS Invincible in August 1984. As in other ports, each visit was met with protests in the city and on the harbour, with the Peace Squadron confronting the vessels.

surfaces.sourceDescription: \n This poster features United States President Ronald Reagan (1981-89) alongside a clock with its hands at 5 to 12 and his controversial joke: \"The bombing begins in five minutes.\" He made this joke to radio technicians on 11 August 1984 while preparing to make his weekly address on National Public Radio. The sound check was not broadcast, but was leaked to the public. \n During Reagan's first term, the Cold War was the most pressing foreign policy issue, and he was known for his tough, anti-communist rhetoric. In 1983, he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan aiming to develop space-based weapons to protect America from attacks by Soviet nuclear missiles. He embarked on a massive build-up of weapons and troops. In 1983, he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan aiming to develop space-based weapons to protect America from attacks by Soviet nuclear missiles. This plan was quickly dubbed 'Star Wars'.

This poster was designed by cartoonist and illustrator Trace Hodgson for Greenpeace a month after the French bombing and sinking of its protest ship Rainbow Warrior in July 1985.

This poster was designed by cartoonist and illustrator Trace Hodgson for Greenpeace a month after the French bombing and sinking of its protest ship Rainbow Warrior in July 1985. 
 The Rainbow Warrior was moored in Auckland when two bombs ripped through it. The ship’s photographer died retrieving his camera. The crew had been preparing to set sail for Moruroa to protest against French nuclear weapon testing. 
 The poster was screenprinted by Chris McBride and Dave Kent of Wellington Media Collective in an edition of 500. Dave Kent's expertise with technique, colour and composition enhanced the original illustration.

surfaces.title: Poster, 'June 28 No Tour Friday'
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Poster, 'June 28 No Tour Friday' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. \n This poster protested against the New Zealand Rugby Union's proposed tour of South Africa in 1985, only four years after the bruising experience of the Springbok rugby tour to New Zealand in 1981. Many New Zealanders had objected to that tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid. Protests had caused obstruction and the cancellation of games, and much violence between protesters, supporters and police. \n Renewed protest activity in 1985 demonstrated that the same issues remained. The proposed tour was cancelled after a legal challenge.

\n This poster protested against the New Zealand Rugby Union's proposed tour of South Africa in 1985, only four years after the bruising experience of the Springbok rugby tour to New Zealand in 1981. Many New Zealanders had objected to that tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid. Protests had caused obstruction and the cancellation of games, and much violence between protesters, supporters and police. \n Renewed protest activity in 1985 demonstrated that the same issues remained. The proposed tour was cancelled after a legal challenge.

surfaces.sourceDescription: Students at Georgia State University and its predecessors edited annual yearbooks from the 1930s into the 1990s. The first yearbook, NOCTURNE, featured the 1934 class of the newly independent Evening School of the University System of Georgia. (Previously, the school had been a unit of the Georgia School of Technology and had appeared in its yearbook.) In 1935, the institution became the University System of Georgia’s Atlanta Extension Center, with separate Day and Night Divisions. NOCTURNE continued as the yearbook of Georgia Evening College (the Night Division) through 1946. Atlanta Junior College (the Day Division) published its own yearbook: SURVEY (1937), JUNIOR COLLEGE (1938/39, not a student-edited publication), and GATEWAY (1939-1946). In 1947, when the University System Center became the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia, GATEWAY and NOCTURNE combined as RAMPWAY. The yearbook continued to be published as RAMPWAY when the institution was known as the Atlanta Division (1948-1955), Georgia State College of Business Administration (1956-1961), Georgia State College (1962-1969), and finally Georgia State University (1970-1992, 1995-1996).

Students at Georgia State University and its predecessors edited annual yearbooks from the 1930s into the 1990s. The first yearbook, NOCTURNE, featured the 1934 class of the newly independent Evening School of the University System of Georgia. (Previously, the school had been a unit of the Georgia School of Technology and had appeared in its yearbook.) In 1935, the institution became the University System of Georgia’s Atlanta Extension Center, with separate Day and Night Divisions. NOCTURNE continued as the yearbook of Georgia Evening College (the Night Division) through 1946. Atlanta Junior College (the Day Division) published its own yearbook: SURVEY (1937), JUNIOR COLLEGE (1938/39, not a student-edited publication), and GATEWAY (1939-1946). In 1947, when the University System Center became the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia, GATEWAY and NOCTURNE combined as RAMPWAY. The yearbook continued to be published as RAMPWAY when the institution was known as the Atlanta Division (1948-1955), Georgia State College of Business Administration (1956-1961), Georgia State College (1962-1969), and finally Georgia State University (1970-1992, 1995-1996).

surfaces.title: NAIDOC 1987 Poster
surfaces.creator: Laurie Nilsen
surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 1987 Poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. Nilsen, Mandandanji descendant, used a palette of warm and natural earthy tones of ochre, red and black to represent Indigenous figures and iconography including a stockman riding a horse in front of Uluru; a man wearing a dhari (traditional dancer’s headdress); rock paintings; a mother and son watching a tall ship; a soldier in a trench and a portrait of rugby player Mark Ella, recipient of Young Australian of the Year in 1982.

The frigates were to be built in Australia with involvement from New Zealand industry, and were part of an Australian initiative to boost naval power in the South Pacific. Many questioned why New Zealand needed frigates, and critics argued that social needs were greater than those of defence. The protest campaign was partially successful: only two frigates were eventually purchased.

surfaces.title: Poster, 'To the French Government'
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary:
Poster, 'To the French Government' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. 
 This poster by the Wellington branch of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament protests against French power and nuclear testing in the Pacific. 
 Between 1966 and 1996, France carried out about 190 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia. These caused reef damage, landslides, subsidence, radioactive emissions, and fish poisoning. 
 The poster features the logo for the Nuclear Free and Independent Pacific Movement. The movement was formed in 1980 to widen the struggle against nuclear testing in the Pacific to independence from colonial powers.

The protest campaign was partially successful: only two frigates were eventually purchased.

This can only increase the risk of New Zealand becoming a target in the event of nuclear war.'

surfaces.sourceDescription:
This poster calls for people to join a demonstration against the visit of French Prime Minister Michel Rocard to Wellington, New Zealand on 29 April 1991. 
 The protest was against French nuclear testing in the Pacific. Between 1966 and 1996, France carried out about 190 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia. These caused reef damage, landslides, subsidence, radioactive emissions, and fish poisoning. 
 Community spirit 
 The poster is interesting for its sense of humour and community spirit - not only was there to be a deadly serious demonstration - live entertainment was provided for the crowds turning up to demonstrate.

surfaces.title: NAIDOC 1992 Poster
surfaces.creator: Heather Kemarre Shearer
surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 1992 Poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. Artwork by Arrernte artist Helen Kemarre Shearer. Of the artwork Shearer writes: 'These are my Dreaming stories from my mother's and my father's country - Arrernte Dreaming tracks. I lived at Atitjere Homelands, which is Harts Range on the white fellas map. Dreaming’s represented are the snake, yalka (bush onion), tjaipa (witchetty grub), honey ant and the seven sisters. Alangwa is shown as a vital food supply which is constant and a strength to and for the people. The hands symbolise the passing down of our Dreaming stories for our future generations.'

surfaces.title: Poster, 'Hiroshima Day'
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Poster, 'Hiroshima Day' is indexed from Te Papa Collections Online. \n This poster commemorates Hiroshima Day, 6 August 1992, in New Zealand. \n The poster features an image of ground zero in Hiroshima. At the end of the Second World War, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Both cities were devastated. At least 70,000 people were killed in the Hiroshima blast, with many thousands more dying or suffering from radiation in years to come. These atomic bombs were the first to be used in war and they kick-started the nuclear-arms race.

surfaces.sourceDescription: Signal, volume 50, number 27 (March 3, 1992). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

surfaces.sourceDescription: Prime Minister Jim Bolger at the podium in Papakura, September 1993. To his left is a larger-than-life size poster of local MP John Robertson."Prime Minister Jim Bolger was in Papakura last week launching the National Party's health policy. Some points in the health policy include improving child health services, improving the health of Maori and Pacific Islanders and improving mental health services. Other health priorities are to look at hospice services, rehabilitation services and replacing waiting lists with a booking service. After launching the policy he then visited Middlemore Hospital to see first hand the problems with the health system." (Papakura Courier, 29 September 1993, p. 5)

surfaces.sourceDescription: Georgia State University Signal, volume 70, number 10 (October 15, 2002). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

surfaces.title: NAIDOC 2005 Poster
surfaces.creator: Benjamin Hodges
surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 2005 Poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. "Sometimes our culture may seem as though it is a heavy burden. Sometimes to exit and gain acceptance in non-Indigenous society, we question the importance of our culture. Would it be easier to leave it behind? But our culture is not excess baggage we can freely dispose of. The sphere-shaped objects represent non-Indigenous society. The New Zealand Prisoners' Aid and Rehabilitation Society (NZPARS) was formed in 1959 to coordinate the efforts of many prisoner-support organisations in different parts of the country. In the 1980s NZPARS was challenged to respond to the needs of Māori, who were increasingly represented in the prison population. This poster, probably from the late 1980s, includes a heading in Māori, symbolising NZPARS's commitment to support both Māori and non-Māori prisoners and their families. The poster shows a male inmate thinking about his female partner and child.; ;
Manatū Taonga, the Ministry for Culture and Heritage; ;

This poster from the late 1970s expresses the frustration and impatience of the Māori land-rights movement in that period. The Waitangi Tribunal had been formed in 1975 to investigate Māori claims against the Crown, but in the first years after its formation it was unable to address long-standing Māori grievances. Many younger radicals argued that te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was a fraudulent document and that Māori had never surrendered their sovereignty to the…
surfaces.sourceDescription: This poster from the late 1970s expresses the frustration and impatience of the Māori land-rights movement in that period. surfaces.sourceDescription: The Signal, volume 81, number 7 (October 8, 2013). The Signal was formed in 1943 by the merger of two student newspapers, The Evening Signal (1933-1943), and The Junior Collegiate (1935-1943). Since 1943, GSU has been the Atlanta Division of the University of Georgia (1947-1955), then an independent unit known as the Georgia State College of Business Administration (1955-1961), Georgia State College (1961-1969) and finally Georgia State University (from 1969). The Signal has been published continuously since 1943, but reflecting the evolution of GSU, its masthead has also had the titles The University Signal, The Georgia State Signal, The Georgia State College Signal, and the Georgia State University Signal. The University Archives has a good run of copies of The Signal, but is missing issues from various years.

"My artwork features three brothers with their land behind them and the horizon before the. Their Elders are reflected in the water, giving the brothers the strength to overcome what lies over the horizon. My work acknowledges the young men and women of today who are across the sea doing their very best to protect their home and serve their country, empowered by their ancestors. surfaces.sourceDescription: Bophana Center in collaboration with French Institute and Center for Khmer Studies (CKS) launches a week-long screening event. Since 2007, October 27th has been set by UNESCO as the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage to spotlight archives institutions, giving them an opportunity to showcase their works in celebration of the world audiovisual heritage. During one […] Bophana Center in collaboration with French Institute and Center for Khmer Studies (CKS) launches a week-long screening event. Since 2007, October 27th has been set by UNESCO as the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage to spotlight archives institutions, giving them an opportunity to showcase their works in celebration of the world audiovisual heritage. During one week, Bophana Center and the Institut français du Cambodge are collaborating to offer, for the first time in Cambodia, public screenings of rare movies on Indochina which were recently restored by the French CNC (Centre national du cinéma et de l’image animée). This movie selection aims to share the history and memories of the people of Indochina and also to raise the question of people’s identity under colonialism. The screenings will start on the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage and will last for one week. On the 27th of October, for the opening screening, Bophana Center will welcome Dr. Henri Locard for a lecture on Indochina; and on the 4th of November, for the closing screening, Ms. Khuon Vichheka will give a lecture, “Battambang during WWII”....

Future Sex was a 1990s magazine based in San Francisco and published by Kundalini Publishing. The magazine was glossy with four-color printing and featured articles, interviews, reviews, erotica, and erotic photography celebrating the zeitgeist of technological revolution, body modification, sexual liberation, and the mainstreaming of sexual proclivities previously considered taboo—from bondage to fetishes to "teledildonics."

surfaces.title: NAIDOC 2016 Poster
surfaces.creator: Lani Balzan
surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 2016 Poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. "This is my passionate expressions of a spiritual connection to the land. Songlines Tie All Aboriginal People Together. Songlines criss-cross and go east and west and they go north and south and they go diagonally and they backtrack according to the journeys of the ancestors. They create a kind of cultural network of stories that ties all of Aboriginal People together. This is what my painting is representing, you can see all the songlines coming together creating our nation.

surfaces.sourceDescription: Since 2004, Blender Basics has helped thousands of people learn the basics of the powerful open-source 3D modeling, animation and game design program, Blender. The 1st edition was designed as an in-house tutorial booklet for high school students. Since its release on the Internet as a free e-book in 2004, public interest has fueled the book's development as the software continues to grow. The 4th edition reflected the program's complete overhaul in 2011 to become more user friendly and competitive with other commercial programs on the market. This 5th edition aligns the book to the current interface and command changes and introduces some new activities, features, and academic standards alignment for teachers. surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 2018 poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. "Witnessing historic and horrific atrocities against our people, lands and culture. Advocating, struggling and taking up the fight for equality, justice, civil rights and social change. From the footprints of the white eye on our traditional lands, to the breast of our mothers, grandmothers to now and the future you still stand proud, strong, influential and inspiring. You are our mothers, elders, grandmothers, aunties, sisters and our daughters. You hold the knowledge, stories, language, culture and our future. BECAUSE OF YOU, We Can!

In Ghana and other regions of West Africa a funeral poster is an important part of funerary ritual. Examining two funeral posters – one about omission and the other about inclusion of names – printed to commemorate two chiefs in two Ewe com
surfaces.sourceDescription: In Ghana and other regions of West Africa a funeral poster is an important part of funerary ritual. Examining two funeral posters – one about omission and the other about inclusion of names – printed to commemorate two chiefs in two Ewe com
surfaces.sourceNotes: In Ghana and other regions of West Africa a funeral poster is an important part of funerary ritual. Examining two funeral posters – one about omission and the other about inclusion of names – printed to commemorate two chiefs in two Ewe communities in Ghana and Togo, this article shows funeral posters as arenas of contestation, negotiation, affirmation, and elaboration of beliefs and conflicting views. The article argues that funeral posters are written with a local audience in mind, which means that they are a very useful source for historical enquiry about how people address the subjects of kinship and relationships among chiefs.

surfaces.sourceDescription: Modernist aesthetics in architecture, art, and product design are familiar to many. In soaring glass structures or minimalist canvases, we recognize a time of vast technological advance which affirmed the power of human beings to reshape their environment and to break, radically, from the conventions or constraints of the past. Less well-known, but no less fascinating, is the distillation of modernism in graphic design. This unprecedented TASCHEN publication, authored by Jens Muller, brings together approximately 6,000 trademarks, focused on the period 1940-1980, to examine how modernist attitudes and imperatives gave birth to corporate identity. Ranging from media outfits to retail giants, airlines to art galleries, the sweeping survey is organized into three design-orientated chapters: Geometric, Effect, and Typographic. Each chapter is then sub-divided into form and style led sections

Modernist aesthetics in architecture, art, and product design are familiar to many. In soaring glass structures or minimalist canvases, we recognize a time of vast technological advance which affirmed the power of human beings to reshape their environment and to break, radically, from the conventions or constraints of the past. Less well-known, but no less fascinating, is the distillation of modernism in graphic design. This unprecedented TASCHEN publication, authored by Jens Muller, brings together approximately 6,000 trademarks, focused on the period 1940-1980, to examine how modernist attitudes and imperatives gave birth to corporate identity. Ranging from media outfits to retail giants, airlines to art galleries, the sweeping survey is organized into three design-orientated chapters: Geometric, Effect, and Typographic. Each chapter is then sub-divided into form and style led sections

surfaces.sourceDescription: Sebuah telaah kemungkinan sejarah baru desain grafis di Normal Baru melalui pembacaan peristiwa-peristiwa sejarah dunia dan kaitannya dengan desain grafis. Tulisan ini mendasarkan pembacaannya pada buku Desain Grafis Indonesia Dalam Pusaran Desain Grafis Dunia (2015). “Peran desain grafis dalam aktivisme dapat lebih dalam daripada sekadar poster dan T-shirt,” kata antropolog desain … Sebuah telaah kemungkinan sejarah baru desain grafis di Normal Baru melalui pembacaan peristiwa-peristiwa sejarah dunia dan kaitannya dengan desain grafis. Tulisan ini mendasarkan pembacaannya pada buku Desain Grafis Indonesia Dalam Pusaran Desain Grafis Dunia (2015). “ Peran desain grafis dalam aktivisme dapat lebih dalam daripada sekadar poster dan T-shirt ,” kata antropolog desain Stanford Dori Tunstall. Desain grafis tidak hanya menyoal visual yang tangible , tapi juga tentang perancangan ‘nilai sosial’ yang disepakati bersama oleh suatu pergerakan aktivisme tanpa memberi sekat terhadap disiplin tertentu. Dalam ranah sosial, keprofesian desain memang bersinggungan dan berkombinasi dengan bidang maupun disiplin lain. Dan dalam sejarahnya, keprofesian desain grafis juga ‘hadir’ dalam peristiwa-peristiwa dunia, bahkan dalam taraf tertentu dapat memberi dampak nyata bagi perubahan sosial budaya masyarakat di berbagai belahan di dunia. Esai ini merenungkan pengaruh pandemi Covid-19 sebagai peristiwa global pada disiplin desain grafis lebih dari sisi tangibility atau visual, melainkan...

surfaces.title: NAIDOC 2020 poster
surfaces.creator: Tyrown Waigana
surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 2020 poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. "The Rainbow Serpent came out of the Dreamtime to create this land. It is represented by the snake and it forms the shape of Australia, which symbolises how it created our lands. The colour from the Rainbow Serpent is reflected on to the figure to display our connection to the Rainbow Serpent, thus our connection to country. The overlapping colours on the outside is the Dreamtime. The figure inside the shape of Australia is a representation of Indigenous Australians showing that this country - since the dawn of time - Always Was, Always Will Be Aboriginal Land." - Tyrown Waigana

surfaces.title: Shadis Magazine
surfaces.creator: Alderac Entertainment Group
surfaces.sourceName: Internet Archive / text and periodical collections
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Shadis Magazine is indexed from Internet Archive as a late-period design-context text. Shadis was conceived and started by Jolly Blackburn as an independent gaming fanzine in 1990. In 1993, Blackburn formed Alderac Entertainment Group (AEG) to publish Shadis as a quality small-press magazine, and brought on John Zinser and David Seay as partners. A year later, in late 1994, the magazine received its biggest success by including a random Magic: The Gathering card in each issue at a time when booster packs of the new card game were scarce; many players bought multiple copies of each issue hoping to find a rare or out-of-print card. Wikipedia

surfaces.descriptionSummary: NAIDOC 2021 Poster | NAIDOC is indexed from the official NAIDOC Poster Gallery. Maggie-Jean Douglas, a Gubbi Gubbi artist from South East Queensland, used the 2021 NAIDOC Week theme, Heal Country!, as inspiration for her winning artwork ‘Care for Country’. This is a bright and vibrant artwork which explores how Country has cared for and healed First Nations people spiritually, physically, emotionally, socially and culturally.

WATCH Images de Chine (1901-1904) by Auguste François Shot at the end of the Qing dynasty, French consul, Auguste François (aka 方苏雅) captured people’s daily life in the streets of Kunming, Yunnan, using a camera given by Léon Gaumont. Cinémathèque Française and the CNC heritage department have scanned the nitrate films footage captured by François. Stream it now on Cinémathèque Française’s online platform, Henri. Suzhou River (2000) by Lou Ye Lou Ye’s impeccable international breakthrough, Suzhou River is streaming on Mubi. surfaces.sourceDescription: My first encounter with the Asian Film Archive (AFA) was completely serendipitous. When I was at the Cannes Film Festival in 2022, I was able to catch a screening of Mike de Leon’s Itim, as part of the Cannes Classics selection. Having seen many older films before, it was not my first time watching one […] My first encounter with the Asian Film Archive (AFA) was completely serendipitous. When I was at the Cannes Film Festival in 2022, I was able to catch a screening of Mike de Leon’s Itim , as part of the Cannes Classics selection. Having seen many older films before, it was not my first time watching one with a ‘restored’ label. The magic of film restoration did not fully dawn on me until I watched Itim though. I was dumbfounded by the beauty of the restoration carried out by the film restoration laboratory, L’Immagine Ritrovata, as the version that I watched a long time ago was blotchy and was of very low-quality. I found that the restoration had maintained the atmosphere and visual signature of the film while elevating the technical ingenuity of the camerawork. Image stills from Itim (1976, Mike de Leon) This screening of Itim , and the entire Cannes Classics programme, opened me up to the world of moving image heritage. It reminded me of what my secondary school history teacher emphasised on the importance of learning about the past, that history is crucial to navigating the present and future. surfaces.title: Education is Power
surfaces.creator: Unknown
surfaces.descriptionSummary: Education is Power is indexed from Malaysia Design Archive. A placard includes a visual image written with texts: “Education is Power”, “Resistance Never Futile” and “Read Banned Books”. Slices of watermelon symbolise the colours of the Palestinian flag (red, black, white, and green), representing Palestinian resistance against the Israeli occupation, particularly significant during the 1993 ban on the Palestinian flag. The black and white checkered keffiyeh print is also a symbol of the resilience of Palestinians. Three individuals depicted wearing keffiyehs are shown holding books in the visual imagery in sync with the message of reading banned books.

In this interview, artist Elsa Wong reflects on how she transposed her research into the film’s three-part narrative, working with a variety of materials and techniques, from sourcing found objects to crafting dioramas, experimenting with 16mm film, and developing a multi-language soundtrack. Tawaran tersebut hasil dari pengalaman dalam memberi lokakarya desain layout dan mengampu kelas pilihan Desain Layout. Lokakarya desain layout yang saya berikan untuk pers mahasiswa. Lokakarya tersebut biasanya diikuti beberapa orang, terutama bagian layouter di media pers mahasiswa dan redaksi. Biasanya tak lebih dari lima orang peserta dengan jumlah pertemuan lima hingga tujuh kali. Sebelum dibuka mata kuliah pilihan Desain Layout di tempat saya mengajar (DKV ISI Yogyakarta) pernah ada mata kuliah dengan nama Komputer Grafis. Dari namanya memperlihatkan jejak era pembelajarannya. Nama “Komputer Grafis” sudah ada sebelum saya bergabung di Prodi DKV ISI Yogyakarta (2005). Dalam pembelajaran Komputer Grafis ada tiga pilihan software yakni Adobe Photoshop, Quarkxpress yang kemudian menjadi Page Maker lalu Adobe InDesign, dan Adobe Illustrator. surfaces.sourceDescription: New Glyphs, New Writings by Another Graphic Typography is never neutral. This publication exposes it for what it truly is: a constructed system — shaped by tools, culture, technology, power, and politics. Structured in four parts, New Glyphs, New Writings unfolds through critical writing, experimental design, and typographic subversion. It questions how we design type, what systems we follow, and whose voices we amplify — or exclude. From rejecting industry-standard software to exploring ornamentation, script diversity, and the infrastructural politics of Unicode, the publication brings together a wide spectrum of perspectives — with contributions by Pentagram, Bye Bye Binary, Margot Lévêque, Morgane Vantorre, Charlotte Rohde, Clara Sambot, Laura Csocsán, Heikki Lotvonen, Rüdiger Schlömer, Lisa Huang, and more. But this isn’t just content — the form reflects the method. The publication consists of four parts: A large folder houses three smaller nested folders. Inside each: three A4 sheets printed recto verso, folded, cut, or restructured; a 12-page stapled booklet; a zigzag-folded infographic; and a double-sided A2 poster. All held together with a textile blue rubber band. The entire object is built on our visual identity system and typeset in Monotesk — modular, monospace, analytical. Every detail is intentional. Every constraint is embraced. Printed in full-color CMYK, featuring our Another Graphic Blue (Custom PMS!). Designed by Studio Studio. Edition of 500. Available…

To mark our 10th anniversary we teamed up with COLLINS to create 100 Tens : 50 interpretations of the number 1 from the Archive’s collection , paired with 50 contributions from some of the most innovative designers working today. We sent out a call to folks we admire—from type designers like Zuzana Licko and James Edmondson , to lettering artists and calligraphers like Julien Priez and Petra Dočekalová , and from graphic designers like Bráulio Amado and Marian Bantjes , to illustrators like Christoph Niemann and Susan Kare . What we got back was pure delight. The creativity and range of the submissions astounded us. All 100 Tens This gallery includes all the 10s designed by our contributors along with the objects from our collection. Click any image for a closer look, and a caption that links to the designer’s page, or the item in the Online Archive. To mark our 10th anniversary we teamed up with COLLINS to create 100 Tens : 50 interpretations of the number 1 from the Archive’s collection , paired with 50 contributions from some of the most innovative designers working today. We sent out a call to folks we admire—from type designers like Zuzana Licko and James Edmondson , to lettering artists and calligraphers like Julien Priez and Petra Dočekalová , and from graphic designers like Bráulio Amado and Marian Bantjes , to illustrators like Christoph Niemann and Susan Kare . What we got back was pure delight. The creativity and range of the submissions astounded us. All 100 Tens This gallery includes all the 10s designed by our contributors along with the objects from our collection. Click any image for a closer look, and a caption that links to the designer’s page, or the item in the Online Archive. Behind the Designs Over the next few weeks we’ll share selected process stories as told by the invited designers. We’re grateful for her enduring contribution to our identity. Graphic design history of one of advertising’s smallest and most overlooked formats. One of the smallest canvases in the history of advertising, matchbox labels were produced economically and at high volume. Varying in size from a postage stamp to a playing card, these modest formats demanded maximum visual clarity. The designers had to reduce ideas to flat colour, simple iconography, and type that could be read at a glance. The printing constraints were severe. Most labels were produced by lithography, often in limited colour runs and on cheap paper stock. This forced designers to produce refined and constrained graphic design in the industrial era. surfaces.sourceDescription: A collection of matchbox labels from around the world. Graphic design history of one of advertising’s smallest and most overlooked formats. One of the smallest canvases in the history of advertising, matchbox labels were produced economically and at high volume. Varying in size from a postage stamp to a playing card, these modest formats demanded maximum visual clarity. The designers had to reduce ideas to flat colour, simple iconography, and type that could be read at a glance. The printing constraints were severe. Most labels were produced by lithography, often in limited colour runs and on cheap paper stock. This forced designers to produce refined and constrained graphic design in the industrial era. The first friction match is believed to have been sold in 1827, following several prototypes developed by John Walker, a pharmacist from Stockton-on-Tees. As matches spread across the world, so did the labels that housed them. By the mid-nineteenth century, match manufacture had become a significant industry, with factories across Europe, Asia, and America producing matches by the billion. With competition between manufacturers, the label was one of the few points of difference available. Like all packaging, it had to identify the brand, communicate safety information, and catch the eye, all within a rectangle small enough to fit in a pocket. Among the highest-output producers, Czechoslovakia, the Soviet Union, and India each developed their own distinct visual styles....

surfaces.sourceDescription: A 1928 article on typographic carnival posters, originally in German, published in Typographische Mitteilungen, Vol 25, No 02, February 1928 This article is part of a series I will be adding to the website called Design Translated. Where I will scan and translate content featured in rare design magazines published between 1920 and 1940. Many of these texts have never been translated before. My goal is to offer fresh perspectives and shed light on forgotten information, designers, and imagery from this fascinating era. This article was originally written in German and English and published in Typographische Mitteilungen, Vol 25, No 02, February 1928 Colourful posters, designed by artists and artistically inclined individuals in every conceivable style and fashion, produced in lithography and offset printing, now decorate walls and notice boards. All sorts of striking motifs and personalities are depicted in order to catch the eye, to arouse curiosity and entice people. In contrast to this exuberance, the pure type poster—or one produced only with typographic material—however skilfully and richly arranged, often appears rather sober, even dull. Now the business of lithographic and offset printing is flourishing, but the book printer too may occasionally secure work, even if not always highly profitable. surfaces.sourceDescription: A profile of British designer Dennis Bailey, featured in Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980 by Ian McLaren and Tony Pritchard, exploring his early influences and role in shaping post-war modernist graphic design in Britain. Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980 Ian McLaren and Tony Pritchard ‘ Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980 ’ was first published in hardback during 2024. As it sold out quickly the authors wish to broaden the readership in the education sector. In a series for Design Reviewed in collaboration with The Modernist Society, we will publish profiles of a number of lesser-known graphic designers featured in the book who helped shape Modernist graphic design in Britain during the post-war period. Coinciding with a second printing of the book in softback the series begins with an exploration of the work of a designer who embraced continental European Modernist design and helped develop the themes which make Modernism in Britain distinctive. Dennis Bailey Dennis was born on the South coast of England; and brought up in Worthing. He refers to being intrigued by amongst other things watching local signwriters. 1 Before the advent of decals and laser cutting, signwriters used the brush. So one can well imagine that Dennis’s typographic sensitivity was informed from an early age by watching this essentially craft based skill. surfaces.sourceDescription: Donated along with their collection in 2016, Emigre’s font development files represent a rare comprehensive view of a digital type foundry’s process. After two years of work, the collection is now digitized in full, a world’s first for such an archive. A selection of objects will be made available to the public through the Online Archive . Archive and Self At the time I joined the project, a number of posters and magazines had already been digitized. Having worked mostly in cataloging and processing at the Archive—and before that as a student worker in the Heller Rare Book Room at Mills College—I was still relatively new to the imaging process. Digitization Archivist Ellis Martin suggested the Font Development Files as a good starting point; the objects were primarily flat works on paper and relatively similar in size, which allowed me to focus on the finer points of digitization while moving through a substantial collection. Process work for Base 9/12 . Process work is special because it provides us with a clearer idea of how typefaces are constructed. The journey from idea to finished object is rarely linear, and its methods are seldom made visible to audiences. surfaces.sourceDescription: In 1972, the editorial board of Typografische Monatsblätter (TM) , one of the leading trade journals in Switzerland, approved a series of cover designs intended to lay the groundwork for the publication’s new artistic direction. Enlisting newly appointed board member Wolfgang Weingart (1941–2021) to produce fifteen covers for the 1972 and ’73 print runs, the outcome inspired both high praise and harsh criticism from a design milieu accustomed to the quiet precision of former art director Robert Büchler (1914–2005) and regular contributor Emil Ruder (1914–1970). Weingart’s provocative covers invited an unprecedented level of controversy by appearing to flout the fundamental principles of modernist design. Instead, his iconoclastic approach struck at the very heart of the Swiss tradition. Marked by rapid advancements in phototypesetting, the early 1970s represented a transitional moment for the Swiss typographic style, as young designers began to move away from the prescriptive idealism associated with midcentury modernism. Reflecting the conditions of a globalized and increasingly turbulent world, Weingart’s work responds to a growing skepticism towards postwar optimism. Sometimes described as “Swiss Punk,” his irreverent approach provided the means to expose the limits of modern typography from within. surfaces.sourceDescription: Lettres Décoratives: A Century of French Sign Painters’ Alphabets Hardcover, 9.5 × 13 inches, 216 pages Get your copy Sometime in the 1820s, new characters arrived on the streets of France. Above boulevards, they changed color and shape across decades of urban transformation and popular revolt. Their captivating forms hailed poets into crowded cafés, embellished neighborhood shopfronts, and, for those roving city dwellers Charles Baudelaire called “botanists of the sidewalk,” turned streets into galleries as fascinating as the Louvre. Thousands of skilled painters saw to their every need. Climate and capital were hard on painted letters, always fading and displacing old signs. Two hundred years on, we sometimes struggle to appreciate their presence through black-and-white photographs and vanishing remains. Yet many have made their way to us in freshly painted glory, preserved in extraordinary nineteenth- and twentieth-century lithographic albums that share the defining alphabets of the sign painters’ trade. Lettres Décoratives: A Century of French Sign Painters’ Alphabets offers a comprehensive look inside 12 of these rare alphabet albums, sharing over 150 large-scale reproductions, together with an eye-opening historical essay by sign painting expert Morgane Côme, detailed commentary on the materials, and archival photographs of the letters in use. This extract highlights the importance that the Central School of Arts and Crafts played in establishing the connection between design education and the emerging professional practice. An examination of those teaching and studying here during the late 1940s and early 1950s indicates the impact the participants were having on the evolution of what would become the design curriculum in many of the art schools that followed. The Central School of Arts and Crafts Art and design in Britain owes a great deal to William Johnstone. The son of a modest farmer on the Scottish borders, he came to London via Edinburgh, Paris and California. When appointed to principalship of the Central School of Arts and Crafts (the Central) during the late 1940s, he assembled a remarkable staff team. As a result, because of Johnstone’s enthusiasm and methods, during the immediate post-war period, the Central was without question the most dynamic art school in the country. surfaces.sourceDescription: In our ongoing effort to expand the story of graphic design beyond the Western canon, Letterform Archive continues to collect objects that illustrate the development of the world’s writing systems. This means consulting with experts in those scripts, as we recently did with Synoptic Office , a design firm working internationally with a focus on cultural heritage and archival collections. Their research into the landscape of Chinese typography appears in The Bloomsbury Handbook of Global Typography . We asked their team to source Chinese lettering manuals that are otherwise inaccessible in the West. The resulting collection, gathered from bookshops and flea markets in China, is unusual for an American institution — and one that we were unlikely to acquire any other way. In this guest post, Caspar Lam and YuJune Park of Synoptic Office tell us what they discovered. At the start of China’s Republican era in the early twentieth century, a unique form of lettering called meishuzi (美術字), or “art lettering,” 1 emerged that was distinctly different from both classical calligraphy and historically printed forms. Hastened by encounters with the West, Japanese imports, and shifting ideas about tradition and modernity, meishuzi developed alongside illustrated magazines, advertising, and the adoption of Western-style printing presses. surfaces.sourceDescription: The Papers, 1933-1981, of Stetson Kennedy comprise correspondence; subject files on various organizations, individuals, and ideas; typescripts of articles written by Kennedy; newsclippings; press releases; bulletins and fliers; pamphlets; periodicals; and photographs. The subject files pertain to economic conditions, labor and anti-black violence, peace groups, peonage, Southern politicians, Mexico, the Spanish Civil War, and Kennedy's own campaign for a U.S. Senate seat from Florida in 1950. Articles, clippings, and pamphlets concern civil rights, international affairs, the Ku Klux Klan, labor (particularly CIO) organizing, and southern politics. The photographs depict WPA work in progress, attacks against Negroes (including lynching), and various organizations. The many periodicals include two issues (1947) of Eugene Talmadge's The Statesman, twenty-one issues (1943-1950) of The Southern Patriot, and eight issues (1939-1943) of Lillian Smith's North Georgia Review. Located in Atlanta, Georgia, Lane Brothers Commercial Photographers existed from the 1930s until about 1980. The collection consists of about 258,100 acetate negatives, 1920-1976 [bulk 1939-1975], housed in 43,486 envelopes organized into 6 series.

memberPages.title: A cobbler who doesn't wear shoes. This hole in the wall is a typical cobbler's shop at Skoplje, Serbia. His own shoeless feet wouldn't be considered a very good advertisement for his trade in America. But he has all the trade that he can take care of as leather is mighty scarce. He didn't mind because the American Red Cross brought several thousand pairs of shoes into the Balkans for distribution to the needy. He says, he realizes the soles will wear out sometime and that means more trade for him
